text: A script that fails silently is worse than one that crashes loudly. More than one automation job at Northbridge Retail has quietly stopped running and nobody noticed for days, because nothing it wrote down said so. This lesson covers Python's logging module and proper error handling, so your scripts always leave a trail and fail in a way someone can act on.

print always prints, always to the console, with no severity and no timestamp. The logging module fixes all three: you call .info, .warning, or .error on a logger, each message carries a severity level, and basicConfig controls which levels actually show — set it to INFO and debug messages get suppressed automatically.

A handler decides where a log message actually goes, and you can attach more than one to the same logger. Northbridge sends everything to a file handler for the permanent record, and only warnings-or-worse to a console handler, so an operator watching the terminal isn't drowned in routine info lines.

Wrap anything that might fail — a connection, a file read — in try and except, so one bad server doesn't take down the whole run. Catch the specific exception you expect, like ConnectionError, before a broader Exception fallback, so different failures can get handled differently instead of all looking the same.

A custom exception class names your own failure condition explicitly instead of overloading a generic Exception. Pair it with simple retry logic — try a few times, log each failed attempt as a warning — and only raise your custom HealthCheckError once every attempt has actually failed.
That closes out Chapter 2, Python for Automation. Next up, Chapter 3 moves into data formats and configuration, starting with working with JSON in Python.
